title: Let's Go to Camp... David!
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck (with Jerry and producer Dave in the banter) explore Camp David, the rustic presidential retreat in Catoctin Mountain Park in western Maryland. They cover its origins as a New Deal project (Catoctin Recreational Demonstration Area, Camp Hi-Catoctin), its renaming to Shangri-La and then Camp David by Eisenhower, the cabins and facilities, presidents' use of the site, famous diplomatic meetings including the Camp David Accords, the Navy and Marine operations that run it, and its security. The episode opens with a cruise plug and closes with listener mail correcting an earlier Roar episode about writer-director-stars in film.
topics: presidential cabins Aspen Laurel Lodge Hickory Lodge

segments.title: Opening and cruise plug
segments.summary: Hosts open the show, plug an adults-only Virgin Voyages cruise from New York to Bermuda in October, and banter about it.

segments.title: Introduction to Camp David and its origins
segments.summary: Camp David is introduced as a presidential retreat in the Catoctin Mountains of western Maryland. Hosts describe its start as a 1930s New Deal project after the Dust Bowl era, when the federal government bought about ten thousand acres of depleted land and created the Catoctin Recreational Demonstration Area.

segments.title: FDR's presidential yacht and move to Camp Hi-Catoctin
segments.summary: The hosts describe FDR's floating White House yacht, the USS Potomac, and how the presidency moved to the Camp Hi-Catoctin site in April 1942 because of FDR's sinus problems. Camp Hi-Catoctin was originally finished in 1938.

segments.title: OSS House of Horrors and Navy takeover
segments.summary: A digression on the OSS using the nearby site to train spies in close-quarters combat in a 'House of Horrors.' The Navy then took over the retreat, and Marines were assigned to guard it.

segments.title: Renaming to Shangri-La and FDR's cabins
segments.summary: FDR renamed the site Shangri-La after the Lost Horizon novel. The hosts describe the wheelchair-accessible design and the Bear's Den cabin, the dog house for his dog Fala, and Churchill and FDR's wartime planning and visits, including the jukebox story at the Cozy Restaurant in Thurmont.

segments.title: Transition to first break
segments.summary: Brief lead-in before the first break.

segments.title: Truman and Eisenhower's changes
segments.summary: Truman preferred the Key West Little White House, but added heating for year-round use. Hosts discuss how presidents viewed Camp David differently, then Eisenhower considered it a needless luxury, until his attorney general Herbert Brownell praised it and Eisenhower kept it.

segments.title: Camp David acreage and renaming to Camp David
segments.summary: Acreage is discussed as roughly 140 to 200 acres within a nearly 5,900-acre park. Eisenhower renamed Shangri-La to Camp David after his grandson, saying the name was too fancy for a Kansas farm boy.

segments.title: Eisenhower's fun additions and the bomb shelter
segments.summary: Eisenhower added a helicopter pad, a movie theater, and a one-hole golf course, renamed Bear's Den to Aspen, and started the cabin-tree naming tradition. Under Eisenhower or in the 1950s, a bomb shelter was built, later reinforced under Nixon, who put a heated pool on top of it.

segments.title: Camp David photos, Laurel Lodge, and chapel
segments.summary: Few photos of Camp David are released, usually by administrations. Nixon built Laurel Lodge, renaming the old one Holly Lodge. Reagan requested a non-denominational chapel, which opened under George H. W. Bush as Evergreen Chapel. Jimmy Carter held Sunday services in Hickory Lodge. The only wedding there was Doro Bush's.

segments.title: Bush Christmases and Obama's basketball court
segments.summary: The Bushes spent Christmases at Camp David, and George W. Bush refurbished the basketball court for Obama before leaving office.

segments.title: Khrushchev visit and bomb shelter deck
segments.summary: Khrushchev visited in 1959 by invitation from Eisenhower. The hosts describe the temporary deck built over the excavated bomb shelter site, the bowling alley's automatic pinsetter, and Khrushchev's shooting gift and license plate.

segments.title: Macmillan and Western movie nights
segments.summary: British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan disliked the movie nights, where Eisenhower showed westerns. The hosts chat about their favorite westerns.

segments.title: Post-Bay of Pigs visit and the Camp David Accords
segments.summary: Kennedy invited Eisenhower to consult after the Bay of Pigs, with a Pulitzer-winning photo by Paul Vathis. The hosts then describe the Camp David Accords of 1978 in which Jimmy Carter presided over Begin and Sadat for thirteen days, and the isolation that helped talks.

segments.title: Reagan, Bushes, Obama, Trump, and the G8 summit
segments.summary: Reagan loved riding horses and used Camp David for weekends and weekly radio addresses. Bushes and Obama used it, Obama moved the G8 summit there, and Trump called it rustic and used it for a Middle East strategy retreat.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the operations segment.

segments.title: Navy staff, Civil Engineer Corps, and departments
segments.summary: Camp David is run by the Navy's Naval Support Facility Thurmont, with Civil Engineer Corps members called CBs. Departments include Public Works, Operations, Supply, and food service. Staff tours are 36 months.

segments.title: Presidential grocery bills and food service
segments.summary: The first family pays for its own groceries, billed monthly, a practice Michelle Obama reportedly described. The hosts speculate about how grocery shopping is handled.

segments.title: Marine guards and security clearance
segments.summary: The Marines from the Eighth and I Street Barracks guard Camp David, with a permanent security company from 1971-72 and about 18-month tours. Staff hold Yankee White clearance, a deep background check.

segments.title: Hosting foreign leaders and accommodations
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the logistics of hosting foreign leaders, including religious and dietary accommodations, cabin assignments, and staff stress during summits.

segments.title: Perimeter security, airspace, and hikers
segments.summary: Hikers who stray near Camp David may meet Marines in the woods. Airspace is restricted to a three-mile zone normally and ten miles when the president is present, with fighter jets intercepting planes.

segments.title: Cabins, facilities, golf carts, and skeet shooting
segments.summary: Around twenty cabins exist, including Aspen with four bedrooms, Laurel Lodge for conferences, and Hickory Lodge with a bar, hookah lounge, and gift shop. Golf Cart One is the president's cart, named by George W. Bush. Hosts chat about skeet shooting.

segments.title: Closing remarks on Camp David
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up the Camp David discussion and suggest visiting and reporting back.

segments.title: Listener mail on writer-director-stars
segments.summary: A listener corrects an earlier Roar episode claim that a film's writer, director and star should not be the same person, citing examples such as Clint Eastwood, Spike Lee, Woody Allen, and Orson Welles.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank the listener and give the iHeartRadio credit and contact information.
